What do we owe people who don’t yet exist? It’s tempting to say: a life as comfortable as our own. But the philosophical literature redirects that intuition toward a different obligation — preserving the conditions that allow future people to flourish.

Why the shift? Two puzzles complicate the simple answer. First, our choices today change not only the quality of future lives but which people will exist at all (the Non‑Identity Problem). Second, standard economic tools like exponential discounting tend to shrink distant harms into negligible present values, structurally biasing policy against long‑term goods.

A concrete example helps: burning fossil fuels improves living standards now, yet it depletes the shared carbon budget and risks leaving a more unstable climate for those born later. Under a rights‑based view it’s hard to claim specific future people are ‘‘harmed’’ when different choices would mean different people would be born. So many philosophers instead frame duties as stewardship: maintain ecological stability, institutional capital and access so future generations have options.

This reframing keeps an important limitation: it doesn’t resolve how much current generations must sacrifice, especially when poorer nations rely on resource use to lift people out of poverty. Do we demand radical present austerity for an uncertain future, or accept some risk to their baseline conditions?

linkedin:
We instinctively think we should leave future generations lives as comfortable as our own — yet two deep difficulties force a rethink. First, our present choices alter not only living conditions but which people will come into existence (the Non‑Identity Problem). Second, mainstream economic practice applies exponential discounting, mathematically diminishing the weight of harms that occur centuries hence and biasing policy toward present consumption.

Because who exists is sensitive to timing and environment, person‑affecting arguments about ‘‘harming’’ particular future individuals face a challenge: a person born into a degraded world might have no standing to say they were made worse off, since under a different policy they would not exist at all. One response to this paradox recasts intergenerational duties as impersonal stewardship. Under models like Edith Brown Weiss’s planetary trust, current generations are trustees obligated to conserve ecological stability, institutional capital and access so that posterity retains genuine options for flourishing.

This impersonal account clarifies why we have duties to the future without appealing to identifiable victims, but it does not settle the boundary of sacrifice. Rejecting pure time preference and lowering discount rates can demand heavy present‑day sacrifices — a contested and practically urgent problem for poorer societies trying to eradicate immediate deprivation.

Given the Non‑Identity Problem and the moral weight of stewardship, how should international frameworks balance preserving baseline conditions for the long term with the immediate development needs of today’s poorest populations?
